nodeData.note: How Kenya's push–pull system (icipe) protects maize and sorghum from stemborers, fall armyworm and striga using desmodium between the rows and a Napier or Brachiaria border: the science, the step-by-step layout, management, mistakes, results and sources. Search: push pull, desmodium, Napier, Brachiaria, striga, witchweed, stemborer, fall armyworm, icipe, climate-smart.

children.note: A Kenyan-born way of growing maize or sorghum between rows of a repellent legume (desmodium, the "push") inside a border of a trap grass (Napier or Brachiaria, the "pull"). It controls stemborers, fall armyworm and striga without any pesticide.

The International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology worked it out in the 1990s with Rothamsted Research (UK) and national partners such as KALRO. It is now used by tens of thousands of East African farmers.

manas.q: Which two institutes developed push–pull, and where?

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: Silverleaf (Desmodium uncinatum) or greenleaf (D. intortum) desmodium gives off smells that stemborer moths avoid, so they do not lay eggs on the cereal.

manas.q: Which plant provides the "push", and how?

children.topic: Pull: trap grass around the plot
children.note: Three rows of Napier grass (or Brachiaria Mulato II in dry areas) around the field attract the moths to lay eggs there instead of on the maize.

manas.q: What is the "pull" plant and where is it planted?

children.note: Conventional push–pull uses Napier + silverleaf desmodium in areas with reliable rain. Climate-smart push–pull uses drought-tolerant Brachiaria cv. Mulato II + greenleaf desmodium for hot, dry areas.

manas.q: What is the difference between conventional and climate-smart push–pull?

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: It works through semiochemicals: natural signalling smells from plants that change where insects go. Scientists chose the companion plants by measuring which smells repel or attract the moths.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2016, J Chem Ecol (DOI)

children.note: No pesticide is needed; the only inputs are seed, manure or compost and labour. The icipe primer mentions small amounts of TSP/CAN fertiliser, which an organic farm replaces with manure, compost and rock phosphate.
Stemborers, fall armyworm and striga weed together cause most maize losses on small farms in East Africa.

Moth caterpillars (Busseola fusca, Chilo partellus) that bore into the stem. The farmer sees windows eaten in young leaves, then "dead hearts" (the central shoot dries), holes and frass on stems, and broken plants.

manas.q: Name two stemborer species of maize in East Africa.

children.note: Spodoptera frugiperda arrived in Africa in 2016. Caterpillars have an upside-down pale Y on the head and four dots in a square on the last segment; they feed in the whorl and leave ragged holes and sawdust-like frass.

manas.q: Which marks identify a fall armyworm caterpillar?

children.note: A parasitic plant (Striga hermonthica) that attaches to maize and sorghum roots and steals water and nutrients. The crop yellows and stunts before the pink-purple flowers appear above ground.

manas.q: How does striga damage maize?

links.label: 📄 Jamil et al. 2021, Plant Physiology: Striga (DOI)

children.note: Poor, nitrogen-starved soils favour striga, and the same cereal monocrop season after season builds up stemborers and the striga seed bank. Push–pull attacks all three at once.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: Each part of the system has a measured mechanism; these are the reasons farmers should trust the layout and not change it.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2016, J Chem Ecol (DOI)

children.note: Desmodium leaves release volatiles such as (E)-β-ocimene and DMNT, the same smells maize makes when it is already being eaten. Egg-laying moths read this as "occupied" and move on.

manas.q: Why do stemborer moths avoid maize intercropped with desmodium?

children.note: Napier grass releases far more of the green-leaf smells moths use to find a host, especially in the first hour after dark when they lay eggs. When the larvae bore in, the stem oozes a sticky gum that kills most of them.

manas.q: What happens to stemborer larvae that hatch on Napier grass?

children.topic: About 80 % of larvae die on Napier
children.note: Only a small share of stemborer larvae survive on the trap grass, so the trap crop is a sink, not a nursery, for the pest.
Companion plants also attract parasitic wasps that attack stemborer eggs and larvae, adding a second line of defence.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: Desmodium roots exude flavonoids: some (uncinanone B) make striga seeds germinate, others (uncinanone C, di-C-glycosylflavones) stop the seedling attaching to a root. The striga seedling dies and the seed bank shrinks each season.

manas.q: What is "suicidal germination" of striga?

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2016, J Chem Ecol (DOI)

children.topic: Striga also loses on nitrogen and shade
children.note: Desmodium fixes nitrogen and covers the ground, and striga does worst on fertile, shaded soil.

Desmodium volatiles repel fall armyworm moths and larvae too, and maize grown in push–pull fields carries more benzoxazinoid defence compounds in its leaves. The full mechanism is still being studied.
In 250 farmers' paired plots in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania (2017), climate-smart push–pull had about 83 % fewer larvae per plant and 87 % less plant damage than maize monocrop.

manas.q: By roughly how much did climate-smart push–pull reduce fall armyworm larvae in the 2018 study?

children.note: Desmodium adds nitrogen and organic matter, keeps the soil covered and moist, moderates temperature and stops erosion.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2016, J Chem Ecol (DOI)

children.topic: Setting up a plot: first season
children.note: The icipe primer's step-by-step layout. Get the spacing right the first time; the plot then lasts five years or more.
Mark plots of at most 50 × 50 m, each with its own grass border; never smaller than 15 × 15 m or the Napier shades the maize. Larger land is divided into several 50 m plots.

manas.q: What are the minimum and maximum push–pull plot sizes?

children.note: Clear in the dry season, plough and harrow to a fine tilth before the rains. Desmodium and Brachiaria seeds are tiny and expensive, so a lumpy or weedy bed wastes them.

Maize or sorghum seed; desmodium seed (about 1 kg per acre) or root splits/cuttings; clean Napier canes or root splits of stunt-resistant cultivars (Ouma II, South Africa) or Brachiaria Mulato II seed; manure, compost or rock phosphate.

manas.q: How much desmodium seed is needed per acre?

children.note: At least three rows of Napier all round the plot, rows 75 cm apart and plants 50 cm apart; a three-node cane with two nodes buried, or a root split, with two handfuls of well-rotted manure per hole. Plant before the rains so it is taller than the maize.

manas.q: How many rows of trap grass go round the plot, and at what spacing?

children.note: Drop 5–6 Mulato II seeds in a shallow 1 cm hole with a handful of manure; rows 75 cm apart and 30 cm between plants; three rows all round. Root splits from a nursery establish more surely.

Maize 75 × 30 cm, two seeds per hole thinned to one after first weeding; the first maize row 1 m from the inner grass row. Keep Napier and maize in alternate rows, never the same row, so ploughing next season is easy.

manas.q: How far is the first maize row from the inner Napier row?

children.note: Make a 1–2 cm furrow midway between the maize rows (75 cm from each), mix the seed 1 part to 3 parts dry sand, sow thinly and cover lightly. One extra row 37.5 cm outside the outermost maize row.

manas.q: How is desmodium seed sown between the maize rows?

children.note: Sow desmodium when the soil is moist. Where striga is not a problem, desmodium can go after every third or fifth maize row with beans in between; stemborer control still works.
Desmodium cuttings with at least two internodes, or root splits from a neighbour, planted into moist soil, establish the push row.
Weeding, cutting the grass in sequence and feeding livestock are what keep the plot working year after year.
Hand-pick weeds in the desmodium line (it is easy to confuse seedlings with weeds), hoe between maize and desmodium, thin maize to one plant, and weed the grass rows too.
Repeat; top-dress maize and grass with compost or manure (the primer uses CAN). Never trim desmodium in its first season.

manas.q: When are the first and second weedings done?

children.topic: Cut Napier one row at a time
children.note: Start harvesting at 3 months or 1–1.5 m tall, inner row first, leaving 10 cm stubble; cut the next row only when the inner row has regrown. There must always be grass about 1 m high to trap moths.

manas.q: Why is Napier never cut all three rows at once?

children.note: First cut at about 5 months just before flowering, 2–3 cm above ground, then every 3–12 weeks; keep a 0.5–1.5 m border standing. Top-dress with compost, manure and rock phosphate after each cut.
Cut for fodder (leave 6 cm stubble) or let it set seed first. A well-kept acre gives 600–800 kg green forage and 50–60 kg seed, which sells well.

manas.q: What two products can desmodium give after the maize harvest?

children.note: Pick brown pods weekly, sun-dry, thresh on a stone with an old shoe sole, winnow, and store in a dry airtight tin.
Chop grass and desmodium together, about 3 parts Napier to 1 part desmodium, with maize stover in the dry season. Two well-managed acres can feed one dairy cow for a year.

manas.q: What mixing ratio of Napier to desmodium is recommended for cows?

children.note: Desmodium is perennial: do not plough it under. Replant only the cereal between the existing rows.

children.topic: Cut back, then plant the cereal
children.note: Cut desmodium to 6 cm stubble and feed it, clear stover, dig or plough only between the desmodium rows, then plant maize 75 × 30 cm with manure in the hole.
In later seasons desmodium can smother young maize, so trim it at 3 and 5–6 weeks; after the second weeding let it grow until harvest.

manas.q: Why is desmodium trimmed in later seasons but not in the first?

children.note: After two seasons of good ground cover, plant the cereal straight along last year's line through the desmodium, or dig only that line. This is conservation agriculture in practice.
With good management the same desmodium and grass border protect the field for five years or more; after a long drought desmodium usually regrows, or the plot is re-established.
The primer's list of mistakes that make push–pull fail.

children.topic: Never graze animals in the plot
children.note: Cattle destroy the desmodium and grass border. Cut and carry only.

manas.q: Why must livestock never graze in a push–pull plot?

children.topic: No other crop in the grass rows
children.note: Do not mix desmodium or anything else into the Napier/Brachiaria rows, and do not let the grass flower or overgrow — it stops trapping moths and gets too coarse to feed.

children.topic: Do not cut all rows at once
children.note: A gap ("window") in the border lets moths reach the maize.
Napier goes in before or with the maize, never weeks after; the trap must be bigger than the crop when moths arrive.

children.topic: Do not plough the desmodium rows
children.note: Replanting is costly and unnecessary; the stand lives for years.

children.topic: Do not expect control of every pest
children.note: Push–pull targets stemborers, striga and fall armyworm. Aphids, leafhoppers or storage pests still need their own IPM.
Figures from icipe's own trials and reviews; local results vary with rainfall, soil and management.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: The primer reports 25–30 % more maize where stemborers alone are the problem and roughly double where striga is also present; a Kenyan survey found about 62 % higher maize yield with 15 % higher costs.

manas.q: How much can maize yield rise under push–pull where striga and stemborers both occur?

children.note: Stemborer and fall armyworm protection begins in the first season once the plot is established; the full striga and soil benefits show from the second season or year.
Napier/Brachiaria plus protein-rich desmodium raise milk yields and give forage to sell; desmodium seed is a cash crop in its own right.

links.label: 📄 Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B (DOI)

children.note: Establishment takes labour and seed money in year one, then costs fall sharply; no striga hand-pulling and no insecticide. Return on investment was estimated at about 2.2, versus 1.8 for pesticides.
The technology uses local plants, so the main barrier is learning it. Field days and farmer field schools are the most effective ways farmers adopt it.
Practical points for East African farmers.
Anywhere desmodium grows well (0–1,900 m, reliable or at least bimodal rain). In dry areas use the climate-smart pair. Ask county extension or icipe advisers.

A phytoplasma spread by the leafhopper Maiestas banda and by infected root splits: regrowth is yellow, stunted, bushy. Plant only clean, resistant cultivars (Ouma II, South Africa) and rogue out sick stools.

manas.q: What causes Napier stunt disease and how does it spread?

children.note: Desmodium seed from seed companies in Kenya (the primer names Western Seed, Kitale) or from push–pull farmer groups; Brachiaria Mulato II from stockists; Napier from clean bulking sites or KALRO centres.
icipe now adds vegetables into the plot, promotes drought-tolerant desmodium lines and fodder markets, aiming at one million households by 2030.
Greenleaf desmodium with sorghum inside a Brachiaria border is the usual climate-smart layout; millet fields can be protected the same way.
Alternatives: molasses grass (Melinis minutiflora) repels stemborers but does not control striga; Sudan grass can replace Napier as a trap.

Midega and colleagues showed the Brachiaria–greenleaf desmodium system cuts fall armyworm larvae and damage by more than 80 % on farmers' fields.
